scenario: AITA For Selling My Former Roommates Games | So a few years ago I was renting this place with this dude and we were on a lease. When the lease was nearing it's end he just peaced out. We're talking took most of everything leaving only the last bit of his half of rent and a few things he said in a note he didn't want to bring with him. Thing with where I live is that if you don't discard of things on your own when you move out the landlord can pay to have someone remove the stuff. We're talking cases of dudes having $250 taken off their deposit just for some dude to take 3 milk crates of things to the dump. It's a rip off. I texted and emailed him for 2 weeks asking to pick these things up or take them to the dump but he never responded. So I took most of his things to the dump but he also had around 60 video games for PS4. So I figured I'd sell them. There is a local game store where they buy used games and they gave me $600 for all of his games. Well cut to last week and I was at a party he was at and we were polite. He then asks how the move out was and I said good, and naturally he asked what I did with his stuff. He got mad when he found out I sold his games but I told him that I tried to get him to grab these things but he never reached out. He's now calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked and legally there's nothing there but now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this.

Roommate dynamics are built on mutual respect, and selling someone’s stuff—even if they abandoned it—feels like a low blow. - **If you had asked him for a cut of the proceeds** (e.g., "I’m selling these because you didn’t respond—here’s half"), it would have gone a long way toward mitigating the anger. - **If the games were junk**, the reaction would be different. But since they were valuable, it’s harder to justify selling them without his knowledge. --- ### **What Would Be a Better Approach?** If you’d known the games were valuable, here’s how you could have handled it more ethically: 1. **Notify him of the sale**: "I’m selling your games because you didn’t respond to my messages. Here’s your share (or here’s the full amount—take it or leave it)." 2. **Offer to split the proceeds**: Even if he was unresponsive, this would show respect. 3. **Donate to charity**: If you felt guilty, you could have donated the money to a cause he cared about (e.g., a local shelter) and told him. 4. **Return the money**: If you’re feeling bad, you could offer to refund him (though this might not be practical if he’s unwilling to accept it). --- ### **Final Verdict: Ethical Score** I’d give this a **0.3/1** (closer to wrong than right), but with caveats: - **Not legally wrong**, but **ethically questionable** because of the breach of trust. - **Mitigating factors**: You gave him chances, followed landlord policy, and it was his responsibility to claim the items. - **Aggravating factors**: You didn’t ask for his consent to sell, and the amount was significant. --- ### **How to Move Forward** 1. **Acknowledge the hurt**: If you see him again, own up to the breach of trust. You don’t have to apologize for the legal side, but you can say: *"I get why you’re upset—I should have asked you about the games before selling them. I tried to reach out, but I realize now that wasn’t enough."* This shows accountability without admitting fault in a legal sense. 2. **Refund if possible**: If you have the $600 and he’s still upset, consider offering to refund him (even if he won’t take it). Sometimes, the gesture matters more than the money. 3. **Learn from it**: This was a tough situation, but it’s a good reminder that even when someone is negligent, there’s still an ethical line not to cross (e.g., selling their stuff without permission). --- ### **Why People Call It "Asshole Behavior"** Roommate relationships rely on **implicit trust**. When someone abandons their stuff and you sell it, it feels like: - **Disrespect**: You didn’t treat his property with the same care he didn’t treat the lease. - **Selfishness**: You took advantage of his absence to make money. - **Lack of empathy**: Even if he was an asshole first, you could have handled it better. Most people would side with him on this one, even if they agree with your actions. That’s because **ethics often prioritize relationships over rules**. --- ### **TL;DR** - **Legally**: You’re probably fine. - **Ethically**: You’re in the "asshole" range because you didn’t ask for his consent to sell his property, even if he was unresponsive. - **How to fix it**: Acknowledge the breach of trust and offer to refund him if possible. If you can’t, at least don’t double down—own up to it. Would you like help drafting a message to him if you want to address this?
